いった こと が あります か — Have you ever been?
You learn the ～た form (the plain past) and use it to talk about experiences (～た こと が あります), list activities (～たり ～たり します) and give advice (～た ほう が いい です).
I get on (a train, plane) (→ のった)
I get lost (→ まよった)
I’m surprised, I get a fright
Have you ever been to Japan?
On my days off I do things like reading and going for walks.
You’d better go to bed early.
I rode the shinkansen for the first time.
To form the ～た form: it’s identical to the ～て form, but ends in ～た / ～だ.
To talk about experiences: ～た こと が あります / ありません.
To list activities: ～たり ～たり します.
To give advice: ～た ほう が いい です.
To tell the story of your first day in a new country.
Mihai and Ana have landed in Tokyo. In the evening, tired, they video call Yuki to tell her about it.
Good evening! Did you arrive safely?
Yes! But we’re very tired. Because the time difference is eight hours.
We walked around Shinjuku, ate ramen, that sort of thing.
And we got lost in the metro! The station is enormous…
Well, Shinjuku station is the busiest station in the world.
Yuki, have you ever got lost in Shinjuku?
Of course! Many times. Even people from Tokyo often get lost.
Oh, Yuki. Have you ever eaten nattō? It was at breakfast at the hotel.
Of course! I used to eat it every morning. And you, Ana?
I’ve eaten it… But never again!
I liked it. It’s a bit like Romanian cheese.
Mihai, you really do eat anything. Where are you going tomorrow?
You’d better go to Asakusa early. Because at midday there are huge crowds.
And today you’d better go to bed early too. Good night!
“ta koto ga arimasu” = (have you) ever done
“tabetaku arimasen” = I don’t want to eat
“itta hō ga ii” = you’d better go
“neta hō ga ii” = you’d better go to bed
What you already know: まって → まった, よんで → よんだ, かいて → かいた. The っ pause and the ん stay the same.
Linked, rhythmic: ko-to ga a-ri-mas. The stress doesn’t fall on こと.
Short: “tah-ree”: たべたり (ta-be-ta-ri), よんだり (yon-da-ri).
1. The ～た form: you already know it!
The ～た form (the plain past, like ～ました but between friends) is formed EXACTLY like the ～て form. Just change て → た and で → だ:
If you know the ～て form (chapter 9), you know the ～た form too. You’ve learned two forms at once!
2. Experiences: ～た こと が あります
The ～た form + こと が あります = “I have (ever, in my life) done…”. It’s like English “I have been / I have eaten”:
I’ve eaten sushi (before, in my life).
I’ve never seen it, not even once.
It’s not the same as ～ました! きのう すし を たべました = I ate sushi yesterday (an event). すし を たべた こと が あります = I’ve eaten sushi (at some point in my life, I have the experience).
Don’t use ～た こと が あります for ordinary things from yesterday: “けさ コーヒー を のんだ こと が あります” sounds absurd.
3. ～たり ～たり します: “…and… (among other things)”
To list a few activities as examples (not the whole list), put each verb in the ～た form + り, and finish with します:
On my days off I watch films, go shopping and so on.
Yesterday I cleaned, did the washing and so on.
The difference from ～て、～て (chapter 9): ～て shows actions IN ORDER, all of them. ～たり gives a few EXAMPLES, in no particular order.
The tense (present / past) is shown only by the final します / しました.
4. Advice: ～た ほう が いい です
The ～た form + ほう が いい です = “you’d better…” (literally: “the side where you’ve done it is better”). It’s fairly strong advice.
You’d better not push yourself too hard.
For NEGATIVE advice, use the ～ない form (not ～なかった): しない ほう が いい です.
To a superior, direct advice can seem rude. Gentler: ～たら どう です か (you’ll learn it at N4).
5. Review: all the verb forms so far
You now have all the basic forms of the Japanese verb. From here on, N4 and N3 grammar will combine them in new ways.

アナ の にっき — Ana’s diary, day 1
Ana keeps a travel diary in Japanese, as an exercise. This is the first page.
3 November. Today I arrived in Japan for the first time.
From Narita airport we took the train to Tokyo. It took about an hour.
It was very quiet on the train. Nobody was talking on the phone.
The hotel room was small, but very clean. The toilet had ten buttons!
At lunchtime we bought onigiri and tea at a convenience store. Japanese convenience stores are completely different from Spanish shops.
In the evening we ate ramen in Shinjuku. It was as good as Kenji’s. (I’d better not tell Kenji.)
We were lost in the metro for an hour. But a kind old lady helped us.
I’m tired, but it was a lovely day. Tomorrow I want to see even more.

あさくさ の あさ — Morning in Asakusa
Five in the morning. Mihai woke up. Because of the jet lag.
Ana, in the next room, was awake too. “I can’t sleep…”
“Then let’s go to Asakusa now. Yuki said it’s better to go early.”
At six, the two of them arrived in Asakusa. The neighbourhood was still quiet.
There was a huge red gate. Kaminarimon, the “Thunder Gate”. An enormous lantern hangs in the middle.
“I’ve seen it in photos. But in real life it’s much bigger!”
Beyond the gate was a long street. Lots of shops stood in a row.
But the shops weren’t open yet. Beautiful pictures were painted on the shutters.
“You can only see these pictures when the shops are closed. We’re lucky.”
At the end of the street was a big temple. Sensōji.
In front of the temple, an old lady was wafting smoke over her head.
The old lady smiled and answered: “If you waft this smoke over yourself, you get cleverer.”
“Really?! I want to be able to read more kanji!”
Mihai wafted lots of smoke over his head. Ana laughed.
Then they each drew an omikuji, a fortune slip.
You put in a hundred yen, shake the box and take out a stick.
A number is written on the stick. You take the paper from the drawer with that number.
“Never mind. It’s good to tie a bad-luck slip here before you leave.”
The old lady from before told them. Lots of little white papers were tied there.
Mihai tied his paper. “There, the bad luck stays here.”
But, looking closely at the paper, something was written in small letters.
“The person you’re waiting for — will come. The important person is already close.”
Mihai looked at Ana. Ana was reading her own slip and didn’t notice.
It was now eight o’clock. The shops began to open. And there were more and more people.
The two of them ate ningyōyaki cakes, looked at souvenirs and so on.
Ana bought Yuki a keyring with a little cat.
Mihai took a photo for Tama, of a maneki-neko cat.
At ten, the area in front of Sensōji was packed with people.
“Yuki was right. It was better that we came early.”
“Thanks to the jet lag!” Ana laughed.
In Mihai’s pocket, the little lucky charm swayed gently.
He still hasn’t opened Mrs Suzuki’s bag. There are four more days until Kyoto.

“kita hō ga yokatta” = it was better that we came
